impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a patent holder's conditioning of patent licenses on exclusive purchases of unpatented products constitutes unlawful tying under the Sherman Act when those unpatented products have substantial non-infringing uses.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed a jury verdict finding Ingevity liable for unlawful tying under the Sherman Act. Ingevity had conditioned licenses to its fuel vapor canister patent on customers' exclusive purchase of Ingevity's unpatented carbon honeycomb products. The court upheld the finding that the honeycombs had substantial non-infringing uses (e.g., in air-intake systems not covered by the patent), defeating Ingevity's defense that the products were nonstaple goods exempt from antitrust liability.
impacts.positiveImplications: Competitors benefit from clearer boundaries against patent holders leveraging patent rights to foreclose competition in adjacent unpatented product markets.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies holding patents must exercise caution in structuring licensing agreements that require exclusive purchasing of unpatented products, as such arrangements may constitute illegal tying even when the patented and unpatented products are related.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law that Teva's headache patent claims covering humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies were invalid for failure to satisfy the written-description and enablement requirements of 35 U.S.C. § 112.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's JMOL of invalidity for Teva's patents covering methods of treating headache using humanized anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies (the active ingredient in Teva's Ajovy product), reinstating the jury verdict of willful infringement by Eli Lilly. The court found that the specification adequately disclosed the claimed genus of antibodies given the state of the art, including known methods of humanization and known anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies.
impacts.positiveImplications: Strengthens patent protection for biologic drug patents by confirming that genus claims to antibodies can satisfy written description and enablement when the specification discloses representative species and references known methods of making the claimed antibodies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors developing biosimilar or competing biologic products face stronger patent barriers, as broader genus claims covering classes of therapeutic antibodies are more likely to be upheld.

impacts.caseName: Trustees of Columbia University v. Gen Digital Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions by comparing function calls in an emulator to a model are abstract under step one of the Alice framework, and whether the district court erred in allowing damages based on foreign sales of cybersecurity software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the judgment in a $185 million cybersecurity patent infringement case. The court held that Columbia's claims directed to detecting anomalous program executions were abstract at Alice step one and remanded for step two analysis. The court also ruled that the district court erred in denying JMOL on damages from Norton's foreign sales, holding that extraterritorial damages were improper. The court further reversed the contempt order against Norton's counsel Quinn Emanuel in a companion case.
impacts.positiveImplications: Provides technology companies with stronger defenses against broad software patent claims related to computer security, and limits patent damages to domestic sales, protecting companies with global software distribution.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the cybersecurity space face heightened risk that claims directed to analyzing program behavior will be found patent-ineligible, and cannot recover damages based on foreign sales of infringing software.

impacts.caseName: GoTV Streaming, LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to a server that tailors content delivery specifications to a wireless device's screen size and capabilities are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that GoTV's patent claims covering server-side tailoring of streaming content to match a wireless device's capabilities were patent-ineligible under § 101, reversing a $2.5 million jury verdict against Netflix. The court found the claims directed to the abstract idea of adapting content to device capabilities, a concept long practiced in the art, and that the claims lacked an inventive concept sufficient to transform them into patent-eligible subject matter.
impacts.positiveImplications: Streaming and content delivery companies gain protection against patent assertions based on broadly claimed methods of adapting content for different device capabilities, reinforcing Alice eligibility defenses in the digital content space.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with inventions in adaptive content delivery face heightened difficulty enforcing claims that broadly cover tailoring content to device specifications without claiming specific technical implementations.

impacts.caseName: Global Tubing LLC v. Tenaris Coiled Tubes LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether summary judgment was properly granted on inequitable conduct in patent prosecution based on the patent applicant's failure to disclose prior art (the CYMAX Documents), and whether the Walker Process fraud claim for attempted monopolization should also have been resolved at summary judgment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated summary judgments on both inequitable conduct and Walker Process antitrust fraud claims related to Tenaris's coiled tubing patents. The court found genuine disputes of material fact regarding whether Tenaris's inventors knew the CYMAX Documents were material prior art and intended to deceive the PTO, and similarly found fact issues precluding summary judgment on the antitrust claim. The case was remanded for trial.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies accused of inequitable conduct and Walker Process fraud benefit from the court's insistence on rigorous factual findings of intent to deceive before these defenses can be resolved at summary judgment.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders who acquire prior art through corporate acquisitions face increased litigation risk if they fail to disclose that prior art during prosecution, as courts will scrutinize the knowledge and intent of named inventors.

impacts.caseName: International Medical Devices, Inc. v. Cornell
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the plaintiff presented legally sufficient evidence that each of four asserted trade secrets constituted protectable trade secrets under California law, including that the information was not generally known and derived independent economic value from secrecy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the denial of JMOL on trade secret misappropriation claims related to a cosmetic penile implant, finding insufficient evidence that the asserted trade secrets were protectable because the underlying ideas were generally known in the field. The court also reversed the denial of JMOL on patent invalidity, finding that the purported inventive contribution was based on the same generally known information. The court affirmed the counterfeiting verdict related to unauthorized trademark use.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants in trade secret cases benefit from heightened scrutiny of whether claimed trade secrets are truly secret and not generally known, providing a stronger basis for JMOL challenges.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies asserting trade secret claims must present robust evidence that the specific information at issue is not generally known in the industry and derives actual economic value from its secrecy, or risk reversal even after a favorable jury verdict.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a Rule 30(b)(6) corporate representative may testify outside personal knowledge for purposes of establishing a prior art sale under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b), and whether the on-sale bar requires that a prior art sale expressly disclose the device's functionality.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of patent invalidity under the on-sale bar, holding that a 30(b)(6) witness may testify based on information reasonably available to the corporation even without personal knowledge of the relevant events. The court also rejected the argument that the on-sale bar requires sales to expressly disclose a device's functionality, holding that a sale of a device embodying the claimed invention triggers the bar regardless of what was disclosed to purchasers.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies challenging patents benefit from the ability to use 30(b)(6) corporate witnesses to prove prior sales even when no individual with personal knowledge remains available, and from a broad application of the on-sale bar.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face expanded prior art risks, as the on-sale bar may be triggered by commercial sales of devices embodying claimed inventions even when the device's relevant functionality was not publicly disclosed or advertised at the time of sale.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims covering non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit partially vacated summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims covering non-uniform constellation designs used in digital broadcasting (e.g., ATSC 3.0 television standards), finding that further analysis was needed under Alice. The court affirmed eligibility for claims in two other patents that included specific technical implementations. The court also affirmed the denial of JMOL on infringement and damages, upholding a substantial jury verdict against LG.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with claims reciting specific technical implementations of communication standards retain strong eligibility positions, and the damages ruling supports robust enforcement against standards-implementing manufacturers.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies implementing communication standards face continued patent infringement risk, while the vacatur on eligibility for certain claims signals that broadly claimed mathematical optimization methods may face § 101 challenges.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC correctly found that Apple's importation of Apple Watch models with blood oxygen measurement functionality violated Section 337 of the Tariff Act by infringing Masimo's wearable pulse oximetry patents.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the ITC's finding that Apple violated Section 337 by importing Apple Watches incorporating blood oxygen measurement features covered by Masimo's patents. The court upheld the Commission's domestic industry determination, validity rulings, and infringement findings, sustaining the limited exclusion order barring importation of infringing Apple Watch models.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders, particularly in medical device and wearable technology, benefit from affirmed ITC enforcement power to exclude infringing imports, providing an effective remedy against large technology companies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies integrating health-monitoring features into consumer products face significant import exclusion risk when those features are covered by third-party patents, potentially forcing product redesign or licensing.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the PTO Director's instructions to the Board governing discretionary denial of inter partes review institution constitute legislative rules requiring notice-and-comment rulemaking under APA § 553.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the PTO Director's Fintiv-type instructions governing discretionary IPR institution decisions are general statements of policy exempt from notice-and-comment rulemaking under APA § 553(b). The court reasoned that Congress provided no legal right to IPR institution, that the Director retains ultimate non-institution authority, and that the instructions do not bind the Director.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from the PTO Director's continued ability to issue and modify institution guidelines without formal rulemaking, as these guidelines often lead to discretionary denials that protect issued patents from IPR challenge.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge patents through IPR face continued uncertainty as the PTO Director can issue and change institution policies without public notice-and-comment, potentially limiting access to IPR proceedings.

impacts.caseName: Ascendis Pharma A/S v. BioMarin Pharmaceutical Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a respondent in an ITC proceeding may obtain a mandatory stay under 28 U.S.C. § 1659(a)(2) of a refiled district court declaratory judgment action after missing the deadline for a stay in its original action involving the same parties and issues.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held that BioMarin could not obtain a mandatory stay of Ascendis's refiled declaratory judgment action under § 1659(a)(2) after having missed the stay deadline in the original action. The court found that allowing a party to refile a complaint to reset the statutory clock would circumvent the time limits Congress established for mandatory stays in cases paralleling ITC investigations.
impacts.positiveImplications: Companies defending against ITC complaints benefit from the ability to pursue parallel district court declaratory judgment actions without being stayed, preserving access to judicial remedies including the § 271(e)(1) safe harbor defense.
impacts.negativeImplications: ITC complainants who miss the deadline to seek a mandatory stay of a parallel district court action cannot cure the deficiency by dismissing and refiling their own DJ action, potentially forcing simultaneous litigation on multiple fronts.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly approved a $125 million class action settlement of claims that the federal judiciary overcharged PACER users by using fees to fund expenses unrelated to PACER operations, and whether incentive awards to class representatives were permissible.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed approval of a $125 million nationwide class action settlement resolving claims that the federal judiciary exceeded its statutory authority by charging PACER fees to fund expenses beyond PACER's operation. The court upheld the settlement terms, attorneys' fees, and incentive awards to the three nonprofit class representatives, finding no abuse of discretion. Hundreds of thousands of PACER users will receive full or substantial reimbursement.
impacts.negativeImplications: The decision confirms that government entities face class action liability for exceeding statutory fee authority, and the approval of incentive awards signals continued viability of such awards in class settlements despite recent judicial skepticism.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in excluding a patent plaintiff's damages expert report under Daubert and granting summary judgment based on the absence of a quantifiable remedy.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the exclusion of Exafer's damages expert report and vacated summary judgment for Microsoft in a patent case involving virtual network optimization technology. The court held the district court applied an overly rigid standard in excluding the expert's damages methodology and erred in denying Exafer's motion to reopen discovery to cure any deficiencies. The case was remanded for further proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent plaintiffs benefit from a more flexible approach to damages expert testimony, with the court signaling that Daubert exclusion should not be used to effectively preclude a party from presenting any damages case when methodology issues could be cured.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a powerful summary judgment tool, as courts may be more reluctant to exclude damages experts and grant judgment based solely on the absence of an admissible damages theory.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the ITC's practice of automatically designating all questionnaire responses in antidumping and countervailing duty investigations as confidential is compatible with the governing statute and the common law right of public access to judicial records.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed that the ITC's blanket practice of automatically designating all questionnaire responses as confidential in trade investigations is incompatible with 19 U.S.C. § 1677f and does not abrogate the common law right of access to judicial proceedings. The court held that confidential treatment must be determined on an individualized basis consistent with the statute, rather than applied automatically to all submissions.
impacts.positiveImplications: Increases transparency in trade remedy proceedings, benefiting domestic producers, importers, and the public by enabling greater access to information in antidumping and countervailing duty cases.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies submitting questionnaire responses in ITC investigations face potential public disclosure of commercially sensitive business information that was previously automatically protected, requiring more proactive steps to seek individualized confidential treatment.

impacts.caseName: Federal Express Corporation v. Qualcomm Incorporated
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether a non-party to district court litigation may file IPR petitions challenging the same patents on the same statutory deadline as the sued party, and whether the Board's obviousness determination was supported by substantial evidence.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the Board's obviousness determination regarding FedEx's sensor-based logistics patent and remanded for further proceedings. The court addressed Qualcomm's filing of IPR petitions on Roambee's statutory deadline despite Qualcomm not being a party to the underlying litigation, raising questions about potential abuse of the IPR system. The court also found the Board's obviousness analysis regarding time-delayed reporting of sensor information to be insufficiently supported.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders benefit from closer judicial scrutiny of IPR petitions filed by non-parties who may be acting in coordination with litigation defendants, potentially limiting strategic abuse of the IPR system.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that rely on third-party IPR petitions as a defensive strategy face increased risk that such petitions will be scrutinized for improper coordination with litigation parties.
